facts.statement: Majungasaurus lived in Madagascar between 70 and 66 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Majungasaurus (; ) is a genus of abelisaurid theropod dinosaur that lived in Madagascar from 70 to 66 million years ago

facts.statement: Majungasaurus had very short forelimbs and longer, stocky hindlimbs, though the forelimbs are not fully known.
facts.quote: Although the fore limbs are not completely known, they were very short, while the hind limbs were longer and very stocky

facts.statement: Majungasaurus measured approximately 7 meters in length and weighed more than 1 ton.
facts.quote: Measuring around 7 m long and weighing more than 1 t

facts.statement: Majungasaurus is distinguished by a wider skull, rough and thickened bone on the snout top, and a single rounded horn on the skull roof.
facts.quote: It can be distinguished from other abelisaurids by its wider skull, the very rough texture and thickened bone on the top of its snout, and the single rounded horn on the roof of its skull

facts.statement: Majungasaurus was first found in 1896, initially misidentified as Megalosaurus, and formally named in 1955.
facts.quote: The genus is one of the first abelisaurs to be discovered, first being found in 1896 (although it was thought to be a species of Megalosaurus) and being named in 1955

facts.statement: René Lavocat described a theropod dentary from the Maevarano Formation in 1955, leading to the creation of the genus Majungasaurus.
facts.quote: In 1955, René Lavocat described a theropod dentary (MNHN.MAJ 1) with teeth from the Maevarano Formation in the same region where the original material was found

facts.statement: The Mahajanga Basin Project began in 1993 with scientists from the State University of New York at Stony Brook and the University of Antananarivo.
facts.quote: In 1993, scientists from the State University of New York at Stony Brook and the University of Antananarivo began the Mahajanga Basin Project

facts.statement: Fieldwork in 1996 uncovered a spectacularly complete theropod skull (FMNH PR 2100) preserved in exquisite detail.
facts.quote: Fieldwork in 1996 turned up a spectacularly complete theropod skull preserved in exquisite detail (FMNH PR 2100)

facts.statement: The dentary described by Lavocat was designated the neotype specimen following a 2009 petition to the ICZN.
facts.quote: The dentary was made the neotype specimen after a 2009 petition to the ICZN

facts.statement: Majungasaurus was the apex predator in its ecosystem, primarily preying on sauropods like Rapetosaurus.
facts.quote: Majungasaurus was the apex predator in its ecosystem, mainly preying on sauropods such as Rapetosaurus

facts.statement: Researchers debated whether the skull fragment originally named Majungatholus atopus belonged to Majungasaurus crenatissimus, initially judging the type dentary too fragmentary for a confident assignment.
facts.quote: Although the name Majungasaurus crenatissimus was older than Majungatholus atopus, the authors judged the type dentary of Majungasaurus too fragmentary to confidently assign to the same species as the skull

facts.statement: It was debated whether the dome-shaped skull fragment belonged to a pachycephalosaur or an abelisaurid, with the latter classification adopted in 1998.
facts.quote: Majungatholus was redescribed as an abelisaurid rather than a pachycephalosaur in 1998

facts.statement: Majungasaurus was a medium-sized theropod typically measuring 5.6 to 7.0 meters in length and weighing between 750 and 1100 kilograms.
facts.quote: Majungasaurus was a medium-sized theropod that typically reached 5.6 - 7.0 m in length and weighed 750 - 1100 kg.

facts.statement: Fragmentary remains suggest some adult Majungasaurus individuals may have exceeded 8 meters in length.
facts.quote: Fragmentary remains of larger individuals indicate that some adults could have been similar in size to its relative Carnotaurus, possibly exceeding 8 m in length.

facts.statement: The skulls of large Majungasaurus individuals measured between 60 and 70 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The skulls of large individuals measured 60 - 70 cm long.

facts.statement: Majungasaurus had short-crowned teeth, with 17 teeth in both the upper and lower jaws, a count higher than in any other abelisaurid except Rugops.
facts.quote: The teeth were typical of abelisaurids in having short crowns, although Majungasaurus bore 17 teeth in both the maxilla of the upper jaw and the dentary of the lower jaw, more than in any other abelisaurid except Rugops.

facts.statement: Majungasaurus was a bipedal dinosaur with a long tail that balanced its head and torso, positioning its center of gravity over its hips.
facts.quote: Majungasaurus was bipedal, with a long tail to balance out the head and torso, putting the center of gravity over the hips.

facts.statement: The humerus of Majungasaurus was short and curved, resembling those of Aucasaurus and Carnotaurus.
facts.quote: The humerus (upper arm bone) was short and curved, closely resembling those of Aucasaurus and Carnotaurus.

facts.statement: Majungasaurus had very short forelimbs with four extremely reduced digits, initially reported as having only two very short external fingers without claws.
facts.quote: Also, like related dinosaurs, Majungasaurus had very short fore limbs with four extremely reduced digits, first reported with only two very short external fingers and no claws.

facts.statement: A 2012 description of a better specimen revealed that Majungasaurus had a robust but short lower arm and a hand with four metatarsals and four very reduced, likely inflexible fingers, possibly without claws.
facts.quote: In 2012, a better specimen was described, showing that the lower arm was robust, though short, and that the hand contained four metatarsals and four, probably inflexible and very reduced, fingers, possibly with no claws.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the skull ornamentation of Majungasaurus likely played a role in intraspecific competition, though its exact function remains unknown.
facts.quote: These structures are likely to have played a role in intraspecific competition, although their exact function within that context is unknown.

facts.statement: A 2013 cladogram by Tortosa et al. places Majungasaurus in the new subfamily Majungasaurinae.
facts.quote: A cladogram by Tortosa et al. 2013 places Majungasaurus in a new subfamily, the Majungasaurinae.

facts.statement: There is debate regarding the phylogenetic placement of Majungasaurus, with some studies linking it closely to Carnotaurus while others could not firmly place it.
facts.quote: Several cladistic studies have indicated that Majungasaurus shares a close relationship with Carnotaurus from South America, while others were unable to firmly place it in the phylogeny.

facts.statement: It is debated whether abelisaurids formed separate clades in western and eastern Gondwana, based on recent analyses excluding South American genera from the Majungasaurus clade.
facts.quote: This leaves open the possibility of separate clades of abelisaurids in western and eastern Gondwana.

facts.statement: Scientists suggest Majungasaurus used a bite-and-hold feeding strategy similar to modern cats rather than the many-bites strategy of other theropods.
facts.quote: Abelisaurids, especially Majungasaurus, instead may have been adapted for a feeding strategy more similar to modern felids, with short and broad snouts that bite once and hold on until the prey is subdued.

facts.statement: Majungasaurus possessed an even broader snout than other abelisaurids, supporting the hypothesis of a bite-and-hold feeding style.
facts.quote: Majungasaurus had an even broader snout than other abelisaurids, and other aspects of its anatomy may also support the bite-and-hold hypothesis.

facts.statement: Majungasaurus had a neck strengthened by robust vertebrae, interlocking ribs, ossified tendons, and reinforced muscle attachment sites to hold its head steady during prey struggles.
facts.quote: The neck was strengthened with robust vertebrae, interlocking ribs, and ossified tendons, as well as reinforced muscle attachment sites on the vertebrae and the back of the skull.

facts.statement: Majungasaurus had a lower jaw with large openings on each side and synovial joints that provided high flexibility to prevent fracture while holding struggling prey.
facts.quote: The lower jaw of Majungasaurus, though, sported a large fenestra (opening) on each side, as seen in other ceratosaurs, as well as synovial joints between certain bones that allowed a high degree of flexibility in the lower jaw, although not to the extent seen in snakes.

facts.statement: Tooth marks on Rapetosaurus bones confirm that Majungasaurus fed on these sauropods.
facts.quote: Majungasaurus tooth marks on Rapetosaurus bones confirm that it at least fed on these sauropods, whether or not it actually killed them.

facts.statement: Majungasaurus likely sacrificed speed for power, having short, stocky hind legs that lowered its center of gravity.
facts.quote: Majungasaurus may have sacrificed speed for power.

facts.statement: Most vertebrae and some ribs of Majungasaurus contained cavities that may have resulted from avian-style lungs and air sacs.
facts.quote: Most of these vertebrae and some of the ribs contained cavities (pneumatic foramina) that may have resulted from the infiltration of avian-style lungs and air sacs.

facts.statement: Air sacs in Majungasaurus may have allowed for efficient one-way flow-through ventilation where inhaled oxygen-rich air was not mixed with exhaled air.
facts.quote: These air sacs may have allowed for a basic form of avian-style 'flow-through ventilation,' where air flow through the lungs is one-way, so that oxygen-rich air inhaled from outside the body is never mixed with exhaled air laden with carbon dioxide.

facts.statement: When rotated so its lateral semicircular canal is parallel to the ground, the skull of Majungasaurus is nearly horizontal, contrasting with the more downturned heads of many other theropods.
facts.quote: When the skull of Majungasaurus is rotated so that its lateral canal is parallel to the ground, the entire skull is nearly horizontal.

facts.statement: The lateral semicircular canal in Majungasaurus was significantly longer than in Ceratosaurus, indicating greater sensitivity to side-to-side head motions.
facts.quote: The lateral canal is also significantly longer in Majungasaurus than in its more basal relative Ceratosaurus, indicating a greater sensitivity to side-to-side motions of the head.

facts.statement: Scientists examined the remains of at least 21 Majungasaurus individuals and found four with noticeable pathologies.
facts.quote: Scientists examined the remains of at least 21 individuals and discovered four with noticeable pathologies.

facts.statement: One Majungasaurus specimen had a broken toe bone that subsequently healed.
facts.quote: One of the specimens was a phalanx (toe bone) of the foot, which had apparently been broken and subsequently healed.

facts.statement: The fused tail vertebrae in one Majungasaurus represent the first known example of tail truncation in a non-avian theropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: This is the first example of tail truncation known in a non-avian theropod dinosaur.
